name: Welaun
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Edwards, Owen. 2019. Reintroducing Welaun. Oceanic Linguistics 58(1): 31-58. University of Hawai'i Press. doi:10.1353/ol.2019.0002 (open-access Leiden repository copy: hdl:1887/79038).
catalog_locator: Sect. 4.1.1 Phonotactics, p. 37, paragraphs 1-4; Table 5, p. 38; sect. 4.2.1 Possession, p. 39, paragraph 2.
catalog_quote: Welaun has a highly constrained word structure. Words are canonically disyllabic and built off a CV syllable structure. All surface consonant clusters within a single morpheme can be analyzed as resulting from vowel deletion. ... Primary stress is assigned to the penultimate (second last) vowel of a word with secondary stress on every second vowel to the left. Stress is realized primarily by increased pitch and length on that vowel. Sequences of two identical vowels /ii/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/ and /uu/ are usually each realized as a single phonetically long vowel. Final /aa/ is often reduced to half long [aˑ] or occasionally short [a]. However, such reduced double vowels still bear primary stress, as expected for penultimate vowels. Antepenultimate (third last) vowels and all pre-tonic (before stress) vowels are usually reduced and often entirely deleted in Welaun. ... [p. 39] When these suffixes attach to a consonant final stem they have the allomorphs -aan and -aat respectively. Because stress is assigned to every second vowel to the left, the result of the allomorph with a double vowel is that stress falls on the same syllable as it would on the bare stem without any suffix.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the word, counting vowels (moras) rather than syllables: a word-final long vowel, analysed as a sequence of two identical vowels (e.g. the suffix -aan/-aat), takes primary stress because its first half is the penultimate vowel (iluk-aan [ˌʔɪlʊˈkaŋ] 'nose', kiis-aan [ˌkiːˈsaˑŋ] 'teeth'); otherwise stress is on the penultimate syllable (fulan [ˈfʊlan] 'moon', lobu [ˈlobʊ] 'mud'). Stress is cued by higher pitch and greater length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every second vowel to the left of the primary (alternating, right-to-left), e.g. ulit-aat [ˌʔʊlˑˈt̪æt̪] 'skin', usan milis [ˌʔʊsa̟nˈmɪlɪs] 'drizzle'. Antepenultimate and all pre-tonic vowels are usually reduced and often deleted (Table 5, p. 38).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions. Author notes that because stress is assigned to every second vowel from the right, the double-vowel suffix allomorphs -aan/-aat leave stress on the same stem syllable as the bare stem (p. 39). Reduced final double vowels (half-long or short) still carry primary stress (pp. 37-38).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word, including suffixed forms and compounds/phrases such as loro mata-n [ˌlɔrˈmat̪an] 'sun' (Table 5). Data are elicited citation forms and a text from fieldwork in the Indonesian hamlets Oele'u and Mahein (Belu regency), which speakers identify as the Raiulun dialect; the rule counts vowels, so long (double) vowels count as two, making it penultimate-mora rather than strictly penultimate-syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Edwards 2019 describes Welaun (a.k.a. Bekais/Wekais; ISO wlh, wela1235) from fieldwork in the Indonesian hamlets Oele'u and Mahein (Belu regency), whose speakers say they speak the Raiulun dialect (named for Raiulun in southern Leohito, Timor-Leste); speakers say the Raiulun difference is 'mainly in accent and pronunciation' (p. 33). Glottolog lists no dialect glottocodes for Welaun. Not to be confused with Kemak (kema1243), of which some Kemak speakers claim Welaun is a dialect ('Kemak Belau'); Edwards shows it is a distinct language.

sources.note: This work describes Rote languages and Meto (the Rote-Meto subgroup of western Timor); Welaun appears only as an out-comparison language of the Central Timor subgroup. No statement about Welaun stress, accent or tone anywhere in the book. Welaun is cited only in out-comparisons (74 mentions, all lexical forms such as hoat 'four', sole 'corn, maize', laa-t 'blood') and in section 3.3.4.1 as a Central Timor subgroup language (Welaun, Kemak, Tokodede, Mambae) in contact with Meto, referring to Edwards (2019) for the subgroup evidence.
